turns.teacherReply: Hi Meher, I’m Arjun, your AI teacher. Today we’ll write arithmetic expressions from word situations. Which part of maths feels most comfortable to you?

ask.text: Which part of maths feels most comfortable to you?

turns.teacherReply: Great, Meher. At a canteen, one sandwich costs 30 rupees and a juice costs 20. What total would you predict?

move.shape: open with one concrete everyday situation — kit contexts: canteen and chai-stall bills, auto-rickshaw fares, sharing a pizza or a cab; ask what they think will happen or which they would pick — a prediction, no right answer yet; any bigger/more comparison: two quantities of one kind, in one unit — a count against a count, a distance against a distance; never across kinds; mention once: at the end they will teach this to Bittu (a pretend new student who missed this class)

ask.text: What total would you predict?

turns.teacherReply: Meher, ab Hindi mein: kul daam nikalne ke liye sandwich aur juice ke daam jodenge. Expression kya hoga: 30 plus 20 ya 30 guna 20?

move.shape: they asked for simple Hindi (Roman script when written): from now on every turn in simple Hindi (Roman script when written), even if they reply in another language; say the last idea again in it, simply, and end with one small question

ask.text: Expression kya hoga: 30 plus 20 ya 30 guna 20?

turns.teacherReply: Meher, word situation mein pehle objects aur unki sankhya likho, phir operation. Sandwich aur juice ke liye expression kaun-sa hoga?

move.shape: one idea only: Write an arithmetic expression for a word situation; objects first, then the symbol; point at the screen only at what the on-screen row lists; never a drawing made of characters; end with one small question that makes them USE the idea — never 'samjha?'

ask.text: Sandwich aur juice ke liye expression kaun-sa hoga?

turns.teacherReply: Udaharan: 3 dance tickets, har ek 50 rupaye. Kul daam ka expression hoga 3 guna 50. Ismein operation kya hai?

move.shape: they asked for an example: one concrete everyday example of the SAME idea, your own numbers, plainly marked as an example; the idea in LESSON NOW is still the one on the table; no new step of the lesson yet; end with one small question about it

ask.text: Ismein operation kya hai?

turns.teacherReply: Meher, “3 guna 50” ka matlab 50 ko teen baar jodna: 50 plus 50 plus 50. Kul kitna hoga?

move.shape: worked example, part 1 of 2: say one step, then ask them for the next step; their thinking, your pace; no new idea

ask.text: Kul kitna hoga?

turns.teacherReply: Meher, 4 tickets, har ek 25 rupaye hon, to kul daam ka expression kya hoga?

move.shape: worked example, part 2 of 2: say one step, then ask them for the next step; their thinking, your pace; no new idea

guard.firstDraft: Meher, 65 kul daam hai; expression likho: 3 guna 15 plus 2 guna 10. Tumne isse kaise jaana?

turns.teacherReply: Chalo, ab expression mein multiplication aur addition ka order dhyan se pehchaanenge. Ab naya situation dekho. Metro card kharidne ke ₹200 lagte hain, aur har ride ₹18 ki hai. Card aur 5 rides ki total cost ka expression likho.

ask.text: Metro card kharidne ke ₹200 lagte hain, aur har ride ₹18 ki hai. Card aur 5 rides ki total cost ka expression likho.

turns.teacherReply: Meher, 290 total sahi hai: 200 card aur 5 rides ka 18 guna. Expression mein pehle kaunsa hissa likhogi?

move.shape: confirm specifically: name the exact thing they got right, no ability words; one idea only: Compare two expressions by reasoning about their parts, without full calculation; objects first, then the symbol; point at the screen only at what the on-screen row lists; never a drawing made of characters; end with one small question that makes them USE the idea — never 'samjha?'

turns.teacherReply: Hi Ishaan, I’m Arjun, your AI teacher. Today we’ll write arithmetic expressions from words. Which football position do you enjoy watching most?

ask.text: Which football position do you enjoy watching most?

turns.teacherReply: Hello Ishaan! A canteen bill has 3 samosas at 12 rupees each and a 10-rupee juice. What might we calculate first?

move.shape: open with one concrete everyday situation — kit contexts: canteen and chai-stall bills, auto-rickshaw fares, sharing a pizza or a cab; ask what they think will happen or which they would pick — a prediction, no right answer yet; any bigger/more comparison: two quantities of one kind, in one unit — a count against a count, a distance against a distance; never across kinds; mention once: at the end they will teach this to Bittu (a pretend new student who missed this class)

ask.text: What might we calculate first?

turns.teacherReply: First write the objects and numbers: 3 samosas at 12 each means 3 times 12. What operation joins the juice cost?

move.shape: one idea only: Write an arithmetic expression for a word situation; objects first, then the symbol; point at the screen only at what the on-screen row lists; never a drawing made of characters; end with one small question that makes them USE the idea — never 'samjha?'

ask.text: What operation joins the juice cost?

turns.teacherReply: Good. The full expression is 3 times 12 plus 10. Which part shows the cost of three samosas?

move.shape: worked example, part 1 of 2: say one step, then ask them for the next step; their thinking, your pace; no new idea

ask.text: Which part shows the cost of three samosas?

turns.teacherReply: The number 3 shows how many samosas; 12 is the cost of each. In an expression, which operation represents equal groups?

move.shape: worked example, part 2 of 2: say one step, then ask them for the next step; their thinking, your pace; no new idea

ask.text: In an expression, which operation represents equal groups?

turns.teacherReply: Multiplication represents equal groups. Now let’s use that idea for a fresh bill situation. Write an expression for the bill: 3 samosas at ₹15 each and 2 cups of chai at ₹10 each.

move.shape: pose the question as written, in their language; then wait
